title: Effects of music therapy on anxiety: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
text: This meta-analysis of 32 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1,924 participants evaluated the efficacy of music therapy in reducing anxiety. Results demonstrated that music therapy significantly reduced anxiety post-intervention compared to control groups. Subgroup analysis showed positive effects across age groups (<60 and >=60 years) and geographic regions. However, treatment benefits were not maintained at follow-up assessments. Findings highlight short-term efficacy of structured music therapy for anxiety reduction, though clinical durability requires further investigation.

title: Music therapy for the treatment of anxiety: a systematic review with multilevel meta-analyses
text: A systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis examining music therapy for anxiety across healthcare and community settings. Receptive music listening methods and combined receptive/active music therapy interventions demonstrated strong effectiveness in reducing psychological anxiety symptoms. Benefits were observed across mental health, medical, and workplace/study domains with no significant subgroup differences. The review underscores music therapy as a flexible, scalable clinical intervention, while noting a need for standardized protocols regarding physiological outcomes and longitudinal durability.

title: Music therapy for stress reduction: a systematic review and meta-analysis
text: A multilevel meta-analysis of 47 studies (76 effect sizes, N=2,747) evaluating music therapy for stress reduction. The study explicitly distinguishes tailored music therapy delivered by certified professionals from passive music medicine. Results revealed a medium-to-large overall effect on stress-related physiological and psychological outcomes (d = 0.723). Larger effect sizes were observed in controlled clinical trials compared to RCTs. Tailored therapeutic relationship and active engagement were identified as key mechanisms underlying stress reduction.

title: Effects of music interventions on stress-related outcomes: a systematic review and two meta-analyses
text: Two multilevel meta-analyses of 104 randomized controlled trials (N=9,617) assessing music interventions on stress outcomes. Music interventions showed statistically significant overall stress reduction. The effect size for psychological outcomes (anxiety, nervousness, restlessness) was d = 0.545, whereas the effect size for physiological outcomes (heart rate, blood pressure, cortisol) was d = 0.380. Moderator analyses indicated stronger physiological impact on heart rate (d = 0.456) relative to blood pressure (d = 0.343) or stress hormone levels (d = 0.349).

title: Music listening and stress recovery in healthy individuals: A systematic review with meta-analysis of experimental studies
text: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 experimental laboratory studies (N=706) investigating whether music listening enhances post-stressor recovery in healthy individuals. The pooled cumulative effect of music listening on acute stress recovery was non-significant (Hedges g = 0.15, 95% CI [-0.21, 0.52], p = 0.374). High heterogeneity across studies was observed. Outcomes varied significantly depending on musical genre, tempo, choice (self-selected vs experimenter-selected), and outcome type (subjective stress vs autonomic indicators). Demonstrates that passive music listening does not automatically guarantee rapid physiological stress recovery.

title: The effects of music and auditory stimulation on autonomic arousal, cognition and attention: A systematic review
text: A systematic review of 31 empirical studies evaluating the arousal-mood hypothesis, which posits that auditory stimulation (music, white noise, binaural beats) influences cognitive performance via altered autonomic arousal. Reviewing objective physiological markers (cardiac electrophysiology, galvanic skin response, pupillometry), the evidence regarding auditory stimulation effects on autonomic arousal and cognitive task performance was mixed and inconclusive. Current evidence linking acoustic property manipulation directly to cognitive enhancements via physiological arousal remains indirect.

title: Scoping Review on the Use of Music for Emotion Regulation
text: A scoping review of 47 studies mapping literature on music emotion regulation (MER). The review highlighted significant conceptual ambiguities between music-induced emotion (passive state) and music emotion regulation (active coping). Most existing literature treats music as a unitary construct without isolating specific intra-musical parameters (acoustic structure, tempo, mode, timbre). Calls for rigorous theoretical modeling of intrinsic acoustic parameters and individual listener intent in emotion regulation strategies.

title: Personality and music: can traits explain how people use music in everyday life?
text: Empirical study investigating the relationship between Big Five personality traits and everyday music utilization. Individuals high in Openness to Experience utilized music primarily for cognitive and intellectual engagement (analyzing structure and composition). Conversely, individuals high in Neuroticism and low in Extraversion relied significantly on music for emotional regulation, mood management, and stress mitigation. Highlights that acoustic preferences are heavily moderated by individual personality dimensions.

title: Neural underpinnings of individual differences in emotion regulation: A systematic review
text: A systematic review of neuroimaging literature examining individual differences in prefrontal-amygdala connectivity during emotion regulation tasks. Neural engagement during cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression varies markedly across individuals based on trait anxiety, baseline executive control, and habitual regulatory style. Provides neurobiological context showing why identical sensory stimuli (including music) produce divergent emotional and physiological responses across different listeners.

title: Music's context-dependent influence on oxytocin, social bonding, and emotion regulation: a systematic review
text: A systematic review examining neuroendocrine (oxytocin) and emotional responses to active vs passive musical activities across clinical and healthy populations. Findings demonstrate strong context-dependence: slow-tempo listening elevated salivary oxytocin in post-surgical and pregnant populations, whereas sad music listening in high-empathy individuals occasionally decreased oxytocin levels. Highlights that physiological and neuroendocrine impacts of music are contingent upon social context, listener empathy, and environmental settings.
